A secondary impact resulting from the removal of endangered animal products from the market is stimulation of the development of synthetic substitutes. The economic impact could result from the creation of a new market product as well as ultimate diminution of the value of the natural product when and if the endangered species is restored to where it can be harvested again. Removal of crocodillian hides from the market or high costs of products made from them has increased plastic simulation of alligator hides. Elimination of the importation of whale oils has revealed the potential of substitute industrial lubricants that will withstand high temperatures. A negative economic effect is the cost of treatment of wastes resulting from the production of plastics and other products used in manufacture of substitutes.
The economic impact of the program on the sporting use of endangered species somewhat parallels the impact of trade species—in fact some of the same species and subspecies are involved in both impacts. The economic value of sporting species occurs through the return they generate by sale of equipment and services. Purveyors in these goods and services will lose sales by removal of endangered species from the game lists. They may, however, regain that loss if restoration of the species is so successful as to allow ultimate use again for sporting purposes. The proposed legislation would grant the Secretary discretion in allowing use of Group 2 species—those "likely within the foreseeable future to become threatened with extinction." There is a distinct possibility that endangered fishes such as the trouts which are capable of producing numbers surplus to the capacity of their immediate habitat could be returned to limited use by sport fishermen in a relatively short time.
